stem: An administrator manages resource group rg-web, which holds a web app, a storage account and a VM named vm-test that a developer created in the portal. She deploys a template that defines only the web app, the storage account and a new Key Vault, using `az deployment group create --mode Complete`. Afterwards vm-test is gone. Why?

choices.text: Complete mode redeploys every resource from scratch, so the VM was rebuilt and then dropped when its build timed out.
Complete mode deletes resources in the target resource group that the template does not define, so the VM was removed.
Complete mode moves resources that are not in the template into a holding resource group named after the deployment.
The new Key Vault replaced the VM's managed disk encryption key, and Azure deletes a VM whose disk key becomes invalid.

stem: A storage account was deployed from a Bicep file and later tagged CostCenter=4410 in the portal. An admin edits the Bicep file only to change the SKU from `Standard_LRS` to `Standard_GRS` and redeploys in the default mode. The SKU changes, but the CostCenter tag disappears. What explains this?

choices.text: The redeployment reapplies the resource exactly as the file defines it, so properties the file leaves out, such as the tag, are reset.
Tags added in the portal are stored separately from deployment data, and Resource Manager clears that store on every redeployment.
The default deployment mode is complete mode, which removes every setting that the Bicep file does not list for the resource group.
Changing the SKU forces Resource Manager to delete and recreate the storage account, and a new account starts without any tags.

stem: An ARM template creates storage accounts in a copy loop with `"copy": { "name": "stgLoop", "count": 3 }` and `"name": "[format('stgapp{0}', copyIndex())]"`. The naming standard needs stgapp1, stgapp2 and stgapp3. What is the smallest change?

choices.text: Set the copy element's count to 4 so the loop runs from one up to four and the first instance is skipped automatically.
Replace `copyIndex()` with `length(variables('names'))` in the name expression so each instance gets its own number.
Change the name expression to use `copyIndex(1)`, which offsets the zero-based loop index so the names start at one.
Add `"mode": "serial"` and `"batchSize": 1` to the copy element so instances are created one at a time starting at one.

stem: A Bicep file declares `resource vnet 'Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks@...'`, and a network interface sets its subnet ID to `vnet.properties.subnets[0].id`. A colleague wants to add `dependsOn: [ vnet ]` to the NIC "so the VNet is created first". What should the admin tell him?

choices.text: It is required: references by symbolic name are resolved only after deployment, so they never control the order of resources.
It is required: Bicep deploys all resources in parallel unless dependsOn is listed, so the NIC could be created before the VNet.
It is not needed: Resource Manager always deploys resources in the order they appear in the Bicep file, from top to bottom.
It is not needed: the reference to the vnet symbolic name already creates an implicit dependency, so the NIC waits for the VNet.

stem: An ARM JSON template defines a logical SQL server and, nested in the server's `resources` array, a database of type `databases`. Deployments sometimes fail because the database is created before its server exists. The database has no dependsOn element. What should the admin do?

choices.text: Add `"mode": "serial"` with `"batchSize": 1` to the database so Resource Manager waits until the server is fully created.
Change the database API version to match the server's API version, because matching versions make the database wait for its parent.
Add a dependsOn element to the database that points to the server's resource ID, such as `resourceId('Microsoft.Sql/servers', ...)`.
Move the database to the end of the top-level resources array, because Resource Manager creates the resources in array order.

stem: Six months ago a team deployed resource group rg-crm from an ARM template; since then an admin added firewall rules and app settings in the portal. A new environment must match rg-crm as it is today. Which export approach should the admin use?

choices.text: Export the template from the resource group, which captures the current state of the resources, including changes made after the deployment.
Run `az deployment group what-if` against rg-crm with an empty template, which prints the full current configuration as JSON.
Save the template from the original deployment in the deployment history, which captures the resources with all later portal changes.
Run `az bicep decompile` against the resource group name, which reads the live resources and writes them to a new Bicep file.

stem: An admin decompiles a legacy template with `az bicep decompile --file main.json` and deploys main.bicep with the old JSON parameters file. It fails: parameter `Security.Tenant.Id` is not defined in the template. The ARM template had that parameter. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: JSON parameters files can't be used with Bicep files at all, so the deployment rejects every parameter the file provides.
Bicep identifiers can't contain periods, so the decompiler renamed it to `Security_Tenant_Id`, and the parameters file must be updated.
The decompiler drops every parameter that has no default value, so the admin must add the parameter back to main.bicep by hand.
The decompiler converts parameters into variables when their names contain periods, so they can no longer receive values from outside.

stem: Before applying a changed Bicep file to production resource group rg-prod, an admin must see which resources would be created, modified or deleted, without changing anything yet. Which TWO commands provide this preview? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `az group export --name rg-prod` and then compare its output with the main.bicep file
`az deployment group create --resource-group rg-prod --template-file main.bicep --mode Incremental`
`az bicep build --file main.bicep` and then review the generated main.json template file
`az deployment group what-if --resource-group rg-prod --template-file main.bicep`
`New-AzResourceGroupDeployment -ResourceGroupName rg-prod -TemplateFile main.bicep -WhatIf`

stem: An admin writes a Bicep file that starts with `targetScope = 'subscription'` and declares a new resource group plus a module that deploys a VNet into it. She runs `az deployment group create --resource-group rg-temp --template-file main.bicep` and it fails. What should she run instead?

choices.text: `az deployment mg create --location westeurope --template-file main.bicep`, because new resource groups are created at management group scope.
`az deployment group create` with `--mode Complete`, because complete mode allows a group deployment to create other resource groups.
`az deployment sub create --location westeurope --template-file main.bicep`, the subscription-level command that also needs a location.
`az group create` for every group first, then rerun the same command, because Bicep files can't create resource groups at all.

stem: An admin moves from JSON parameters files to a `prod.bicepparam` file that begins with `using './main.bicep'`. He runs `az deployment group create -g rg-prod --template-file main.bicep --parameters prod.bicepparam` and gets "Only a .bicep file is allowed with a .bicepparam file". What fixes it?

choices.text: Remove the --template-file switch and pass only `--parameters prod.bicepparam`, because the using statement already names the Bicep file.
Remove the using line from prod.bicepparam, because a parameters file that names its own template conflicts with --template-file.
Rename prod.bicepparam to prod.parameters.json, because the Azure CLI accepts only JSON parameters files for Bicep deployments.
Compile main.bicep to JSON with `az bicep build` first, because a .bicepparam file can be used only with an ARM JSON template.

stem: An ARM template hard-codes `"sku": { "name": "Standard_LRS" }` for a storage account. The admin must let each deployment choose Standard_LRS or Standard_GRS, keeping LRS as the default and rejecting other values. Which TWO edits are required? (Select TWO)

choices.text: In the outputs section, add an output named storageSku of type string whose value is the SKU name that the account was deployed with.
In the storage account resource, change the sku name to `[parameters('storageSku')]` so the deployment uses the value passed in.
In the variables section, add storageSku with the value Standard_LRS and an allowedValues array that lists the two permitted SKU names.
In the storage account resource, add a dependsOn entry for storageSku so the SKU value is resolved before the account is created.
In the parameters section, add storageSku of type string with defaultValue Standard_LRS and allowedValues listing Standard_LRS and Standard_GRS.

stem: A Bicep file deploys a VM and declares `param adminPassword string`. A security review finds the password in plain text in the portal's deployment history for rg-app. The password must still be passed at deploy time. What change should the admin make to the Bicep file?

choices.text: Move the password into a variable with the same value, because variables are never shown in the deployment history in the portal.
Add `@minLength(12)` to the adminPassword parameter, because length-checked parameters are masked in deployment history automatically.
Add an output that returns the password through the `listKeys()` function, which replaces the stored value with a key reference.
Add the `@secure()` decorator to the adminPassword parameter, so Resource Manager treats the value as sensitive and doesn't log or show it.

stem: A Bicep file in a deployment named `stgDeploy` ends with `output blobEndpoint string = stg.properties.primaryEndpoints.blob`. A week later a script must read that value for rg-data without redeploying. Which command should the admin use?

choices.text: `az deployment group show -g rg-data -n stgDeploy --query properties.outputs.blobEndpoint.value`, which reads it from the deployment history.
`az storage account show-connection-string --resource-group rg-data`, which reads the outputs saved by the last deployment to the resource group.
`az deployment group what-if -g rg-data --template-file main.bicep`, which reruns the file in preview and prints every output value it returns.
`az group export --name rg-data`, which writes the template of the resource group with the outputs of earlier deployments filled in.

stem: A Bicep file updates 10 web apps in a loop: `resource sites '...' = [for name in appNames: {...}]`. For a production change, the admin wants Resource Manager to update only two apps at a time and start the next pair after the previous pair finishes. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Adding `dependsOn: [ sites ]` inside the loop body makes each app wait for the previous one and limits the run to two at a time.
With a batch size, Resource Manager creates a dependency on earlier instances, so it starts a batch only after the previous one ends.
Without a decorator, the loop instances deploy one at a time in the array order, so the change only needs a smaller array per run.
Setting `--mode Complete` on the deployment command makes Resource Manager process loop instances in pairs instead of all at once.
Adding the `@batchSize(2)` decorator directly above the resource loop makes Resource Manager deploy the instances in batches of two.

stem: A company runs an internal web app in a Basic B1 App Service plan. The team now needs a staging deployment slot for zero-downtime releases and rule-based autoscale on CPU percentage. It wants the lowest-cost tier that provides both features. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Scale the plan down to the Shared tier and enable autoscale there, since Shared apps already get CPU quotas per app
Keep the Basic tier and raise the instance count to three, because Basic supports slots once more than one instance runs
Scale the plan up to the IsolatedV2 tier, because slots and autoscale need an App Service Environment in a virtual network
Scale the plan up to the Standard tier, which adds deployment slots and rule-based autoscale on top of the Basic features

stem: A reporting app runs in a Standard S1 plan. Each report request loads a large dataset into memory, and single requests fail with out-of-memory errors. The administrator scaled out from 2 to 5 instances, but the same requests still fail. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Add a staging deployment slot and route half of the traffic to it, so that each slot handles a smaller share of the requests
Enable per-app scaling on the plan, so that the reporting app gets its own VM memory separate from the other apps in the plan
Scale the plan up to a tier and size with more memory per instance, because each request is limited by one instance's memory
Scale out further to the Standard maximum of 10 instances, because spreading the requests across more VMs adds more memory

stem: An App Service plan has autoscale rules: scale out by 1 if CPU > 75% or memory > 75%; scale in by 1 if CPU < 30%, and scale in by 1 if memory < 50%. Overnight, CPU stays near 20% and memory near 60%, yet the plan stays at 6 instances. Why does autoscale not scale in?

choices.text: The default instance count of the profile is 6, and autoscale never scales below the default while metrics are available
The cooldown after the last scale-out blocks every scale-in action until the next daily profile starts the following day
A scale-in action needs every scale-in rule in the profile to be met, and the memory condition below 50% is not met
App Service plans support scale-out rules only, so scaling in must be done manually or by a separate scheduled runbook

stem: A Standard S3 App Service plan autoscales between 4 and 10 instances for a busy storefront app. A small admin app in the same plan should never run on more than 2 of those instances, while the storefront keeps using all of them. What should the administrator configure?

choices.text: Enable per-app scaling on the plan and set the admin app's number of workers to 2, leaving the storefront app without a limit
Move the admin app into a deployment slot of the storefront app, because slots run on a fixed subset of two plan instances
Add a separate autoscale setting to the admin app with a maximum of 2 instances, since each app in a plan can autoscale alone
Set the admin app's Traffic % to 20 in the deployment slots page, so that it receives requests on only two of the instances

stem: An administrator wants to move a .NET app from its Windows App Service plan in resource group rg-legacy to an existing Linux plan in rg-web, in the same region. In the app's Change App Service plan pane, the Linux plan is not listed. What is the reason?

choices.text: The Change App Service plan pane lists Linux plans only after the app's stack setting is changed to a Linux runtime version
The Linux plan is hidden until the administrator is granted the Website Contributor role on the rg-web resource group itself
The Linux plan must first be scaled to the same pricing tier as the Windows plan, because moves require identical tiers
An app can move only to a plan in the same resource group and region with the same OS type, so this move is not supported

stem: A Standard-tier app serves www.contoso.com and the root domain contoso.com, with access restrictions that allow only the company's office IP ranges. A free App Service managed certificate is created for www.contoso.com, but creation fails for contoso.com. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Request the managed certificate for *.contoso.com instead, because one wildcard managed certificate covers the root domain
Secure contoso.com with a certificate from another source, such as an App Service certificate or a Key Vault certificate
Scale the plan up to Premium v3, because free managed certificates for root domains are only issued on Premium tiers
Replace the A record for contoso.com with a CNAME record that points directly to the app's azurewebsites.net host name

stem: A company runs about 30 customer subdomains such as a.contoso.com and b.contoso.com on one App Service app and adds new ones weekly. It wants one wildcard certificate for *.contoso.com bound to these domains. Which TWO ways can provide this certificate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Bind the app's default *.azurewebsites.net certificate to the contoso.com subdomains with an IP-based SSL binding type
Upload the wildcard certificate as a .cer file under Public key certificates and select it in the custom domain binding
Import a wildcard certificate that the company stores in Azure Key Vault, after granting App Service read access to the vault
Create a free App Service managed certificate for *.contoso.com and let App Service renew it automatically each period
Upload a password-protected PFX file of a wildcard certificate from a CA, including the intermediate and root certificates

stem: An administrator is adding the root domain fabrikam.com as a custom domain to an App Service app. The domain's DNS is hosted at a third-party registrar. Following Microsoft's guidance, which TWO DNS records should be created at the registrar? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An A record for the host @ whose value is the app's IP address shown in the Add custom domain dialog
A TXT record for the host asuid.www whose value is the domain verification ID shown in the Add custom domain dialog
An MX record for the host @ whose value is the app's default host name, so that App Service can validate the domain
A CNAME record for the host @ whose value is the app's default host name, such as fabrikam-web.azurewebsites.net
A TXT record for the host asuid whose value is the domain verification ID shown in the Add custom domain dialog

stem: An audit of a payment app finds that it accepts TLS 1.0 connections from a setting made years ago for a retired partner, and that it still answers plain HTTP requests on its custom domain. Which TWO settings fix both findings? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Change the custom domain's binding from SNI SSL to IP-based SSL so that the app gets a dedicated TLS address
Set the app's minimum inbound TLS version to 1.2 so that clients that offer only TLS 1.0 or 1.1 are rejected
Enable end-to-end TLS encryption so that traffic from the front ends to the app's workers is encrypted as well
Set client certificate mode to Required so that browsers must present a certificate before the app answers HTTP
Turn on HTTPS Only so that every HTTP request to the app is redirected to the matching HTTPS address instead

stem: A Standard-tier app has only the automatic backups. Compliance now requires monthly backups kept for 90 days and copies that the team can download for an offline archive. What should the administrator configure?

choices.text: A longer retention period on the automatic backups, and then export each one from the Backups page as a ZIP
A second deployment slot that receives a nightly restore of production, so the slot acts as the backup copy
A scale up to a Premium tier, because Premium extends automatic backup retention to 90 days and adds downloads
Custom scheduled backups to a storage account container, with backup retention set to keep them indefinitely

stem: Custom backups of a Premium v3 web app worked until the security team set the target storage account's firewall to allow only selected virtual networks. Now every backup fails with a storage access error. Which change restores the backups while keeping the firewall?

choices.text: Integrate the app with a VNet subnet the storage firewall allows, then enable backup and restore over virtual network integration
Create a private endpoint for the web app in the virtual network that the storage firewall allows, then rerun the backup job
Switch the app to automatic backups and point them at the same storage account, because automatic backups use trusted access
Assign the app's system-assigned managed identity the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the backup storage account itself

stem: A web app in a Premium v3 plan must call a REST API on a VM at 10.20.1.4 in the VNet vnet-prod, which has no public IP address. The web app itself must stay reachable from the internet. What should the administrator configure on the app?

choices.text: An IP-based SSL binding on the app, so that the app gets a dedicated IP address that the VM's network security group can allow
A private endpoint for the app in a subnet of vnet-prod, so that the app's calls to the VM leave from a private IP in that subnet
Virtual network integration with an empty subnet of vnet-prod delegated to Microsoft.Web/serverFarms for the app's outbound calls
An access restriction rule of type Virtual Network for the VM's subnet, with the Microsoft.Web service endpoint enabled on it

stem: An administrator created a private endpoint for app-hr in vnet-corp and disabled public network access. VMs in vnet-corp use Azure-provided DNS, and when they browse to app-hr.azurewebsites.net they get HTTP 403 errors. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Add an access restriction rule that allows the VM subnet of vnet-corp, because private endpoint traffic is still evaluated by those rules
Create a privatelink.azurewebsites.net private DNS zone linked to vnet-corp with an A record for app-hr pointing to the endpoint IP
Re-enable public network access on app-hr, because a private endpoint answers only after the public endpoint has validated the client
Enable virtual network integration for app-hr in vnet-corp, because the private endpoint carries traffic only after the app joins the VNet

stem: A web app is published through the company's Azure Front Door profile. The administrator must make the app reject any request that does not come through that specific Front Door profile, including requests sent through other customers' Front Door profiles. Which access restriction should be added?

choices.text: An Allow rule of type Virtual Network for the Front Door subnet, with the Microsoft.Web service endpoint enabled on that subnet
An Allow rule with the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag only, because that tag lists the IP ranges of the company's own profile
An Allow rule with an X-Forwarded-Host header filter set to the app's host name and no source IP range or service tag in the rule
An Allow rule with the AzureFrontDoor.Backend service tag and an X-Azure-FDID header filter set to the profile's Front Door ID

stem: An app has a staging slot whose connection string SqlDb points to the test database. After the team swapped staging into production, the production app started writing orders to the test database. How should the administrator prevent this on future swaps?

choices.text: Turn on auto swap for the staging slot, because an automatic swap leaves connection strings out of the swap operation
Use swap with preview for every release, because a preview swap keeps the production slot's own connection strings
Move the connection string from the Connection strings section into App settings, since app settings never swap
Mark the SqlDb connection string as a deployment slot setting in each slot, with each slot keeping its own database value

stem: A pipeline swaps a staging slot into production after each deployment. The app answers / at once, before its caches are loaded. Its /health endpoint responds only after cache loading ends: 200 on success, 503 on failure. How can every swap warm up through /health and stop unless it returns 200, without a manual step?

choices.text: Turn on Always On for the staging slot, so its instances are fully loaded before the pipeline starts the swap
Set WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH to /health and WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_STATUSES to 200 on the slot
Use swap with preview in the pipeline, because its first phase checks that /health answers 200 on all instances
Set the staging slot's Traffic % to 100 for two minutes before the swap, so real requests fill the app's caches

stem: Storage account `stfabdata` in West Europe allows public access only from selected virtual networks and IP addresses. VMs in subnet `app` of a West Europe virtual network reach the internet through a NAT gateway with public IP `20.50.10.4`. The admin added an IP network rule for `20.50.10.4`, but the VMs still get 403 errors on blob requests. What should the admin do?

choices.text: Enable the exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to reach the storage account from the VMs.
Replace the IP rule with one for the subnet's private range `10.20.1.0/24` so the firewall matches the VMs' real addresses.
Add a virtual network rule for subnet `app` and enable a service endpoint for Azure Storage on that subnet.
Enter the NAT gateway address as the CIDR range `20.50.10.4/32` instead of a single address so outbound traffic matches.

stem: A small accounting firm restricts its storage account to selected networks. Staff in its office must use Azure Storage Explorer against the account. The office LAN is `192.168.40.0/24` and all outbound traffic leaves through a firewall that translates it to `203.0.113.25`. What should the administrator configure?

choices.text: An IP network rule for `203.0.113.25`, the public address that the office firewall uses for all of its outbound traffic.
An IP network rule for `192.168.40.0/24`, because the storage firewall evaluates the original LAN address of each client device.
A resource instance rule that names the office firewall appliance, so its translated traffic is matched by resource identity.
SAS tokens with `sip=192.168.40.0/24` for each user, because a SAS IP limit opens the storage firewall for those addresses.

stem: An admin creates a diagnostic setting that archives Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit logs to storage account `stauditlogs`. The account allows public access only from one virtual network, and no logs arrive. The admin must not open the account to the internet. What should the admin change on the storage account?

choices.text: Enable the network exceptions for logging and metrics so that log files and metrics tables can be accessed.
Add IP network rules for the Azure Monitor outbound address ranges in the same region as the storage account.
Add a resource instance rule for Azure Monitor and give that resource instance a data role on the account.
Enable the exception that allows Azure services on the trusted services list to access this storage account.

stem: An Azure AI Search service must index PDFs in a blob container. The storage account allows public access only from selected networks, and the search service isn't deployed in any virtual network. Both resources are in the same tenant, and the search service has a system-assigned managed identity. Which TWO actions give the search service access? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Assign the Reader role on the storage account to the search service's managed identity at account scope.
Enable a storage service endpoint on the subnet that the search service uses to reach Azure Storage.
Assign the Storage Blob Data Reader role on the storage account to the search service's managed identity.
Add an IP network rule for the outbound public address of the search service in the account's region.
Add a resource instance rule on the storage account for that specific Azure AI Search service.

stem: A storage account allows public access only from the office's public IP. Working from home, an admin opens the account in the Azure portal: the list of blob containers appears, but opening a container to browse its blobs fails with an access error. She has the Owner role. What explains this?

choices.text: The container's anonymous access level is set to Private, which hides blob listings from anyone outside the allowed IP range.
The firewall filters only data plane requests; the container list can come through the control plane, but browsing blobs is a data request.
The portal lists containers with her Entra token but browses blobs with Shared Key, and the firewall rejects only key-signed requests.
The portal caches the container list from the last session in the office, so the list appears even though no live request succeeded.

stem: A logistics partner must upload files to container `intake` for the next three days through a URL, without signing in. Security policy says no SAS may be signed with a storage account key, and every SAS must trace back to a Microsoft Entra identity. The admin has the Storage Blob Data Contributor role. What should the admin create?

choices.text: A user delegation SAS for the container, created with `--auth-mode login --as-user` and a three-day expiry time.
An account SAS limited to the blob service and container and object resource types, with a three-day expiry time.
A service SAS for the container that references a stored access policy with write permission and a three-day expiry.
A service SAS on the container created from the portal's Shared access tokens page with the signing method set to key1.

stem: A third-party monitoring tool must call Get Service Properties and Get Service Stats on both the Blob and Queue services of one storage account, using a single token, without being given an access key. Which type of SAS should the admin issue?

choices.text: A user delegation SAS for the blob service, created by an admin who holds Storage Blob Data Reader.
A service SAS that references a stored access policy granting read access on every container.
A service SAS on each container and queue, with read permission and a short expiry for each token.
An account SAS with `ss=bq`, `srt=s` and read permission, signed with one of the account keys.

stem: An admin issues an account SAS to an outside auditor. The token must be usable only from the auditor's office range `198.51.100.16` to `198.51.100.31`, and it must never be accepted over plain HTTP. Which TWO settings should the admin include in the SAS? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Leave `spr` at its default, which already allows HTTPS only.
Bind the token to a stored access policy that lists the range.
Set `srt=s` so the token works only from the auditor's network.
Set `spr=https` so that only HTTPS requests are accepted.

stem: A team issued 40 service SAS URLs for container `reports`, all referencing the stored access policy `partner-read`. The partner contract ends today, and all 40 URLs must stop working. Internal apps use a connection string with key1 and must keep running. What should the admin do?

choices.text: Configure a SAS expiration policy with an upper limit of one hour on the storage account that holds the container.
Delete the `partner-read` stored access policy, or set its expiry time to a value in the past, on the container.
Regenerate key1 so that every SAS signed with it becomes invalid, then update the apps with the new key.
Run `az storage account revoke-delegation-keys` on the account to invalidate the partner's SAS tokens.

stem: An ad hoc account SAS signed with key1 was posted in a public code repository. Production apps use a connection string with key1, and a few batch jobs already use key2. The admin must invalidate the leaked SAS with no app outage. Which sequence should the admin follow?

choices.text: Delete every stored access policy on the account's containers, then regenerate key2 to remove anything still valid.
Run `az storage account revoke-delegation-keys`, then set a key expiration policy so both keys rotate in the future.
Move the production apps to key2, confirm they work, then regenerate key1 to invalidate the leaked account SAS.
Regenerate key1 right away, then update the production apps to the new key1 value as quickly as possible afterwards.

stem: A developer created a user delegation SAS with read and list access on container `designs`, valid for six days, and it was emailed to the wrong recipient. The storage account keys have never been used to sign anything. How can the admin invalidate this SAS?

choices.text: Set `AllowSharedKeyAccess` to false on the storage account so that SAS tokens are refused for every service.
Delete the stored access policy that the user delegation SAS references on container `designs` to end its access.
Regenerate key1 and key2 on the storage account so that every outstanding SAS issued for the account is invalidated.
Run `az storage account revoke-delegation-keys` on the storage account so the key that signed the SAS is revoked.

stem: To meet an audit finding, an admin plans to set `AllowSharedKeyAccess` to false on a storage account that holds only blob containers. Which TWO kinds of client requests will keep working after the change? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A partner script that uploads with a service SAS created on the container from the account's key1.
A reporting job that connects with a connection string that contains the account name and key2.
A mobile app that downloads blobs with a user delegation SAS issued by a back-end service.
A backup tool that uses an account SAS with blob and object access issued last week.
A web app that reads blobs with its managed identity, which holds the Storage Blob Data Reader role.

stem: An admin who has the Owner role wants the portal to remind her every 60 days to rotate the access keys of an old storage account. On the Access keys page the Set rotation reminder button is grayed out. What should she do first?

choices.text: Assign herself the Storage Account Key Operator Service Role so the reminder setting becomes editable.
Regenerate key1 and key2 once each so that the account records a creation time for both of its keys.
Enable a SAS expiration policy on the account, because key reminders depend on the SAS policy settings.
Store both access keys as secrets in Azure Key Vault so that the account can track the age of each key.

stem: A firm syncs its on-premises AD DS users to Microsoft Entra ID with Microsoft Entra Connect Sync. Staff laptops are Microsoft Entra hybrid joined and often work from home without VPN. Users must reach an SMB Azure file share with their own identities, and clients have no line of sight to domain controllers. Which identity source should the admin enable?

choices.text: Microsoft Entra Kerberos authentication, with admin consent granted to the storage account's application.
No identity source; mount the share from a logon script that passes the storage account key as the password.
On-premises AD DS authentication, registering the storage account in the domain with the AzFilesHybrid module.
Microsoft Entra Domain Services authentication, with the laptops joined to the managed domain for Kerberos.

stem: An Azure file share uses AD DS authentication. Hybrid user Mia has the Storage File Data SMB Share Reader role on the share and the NTFS Modify permission on folder `\Projects`. She can open files there but can't save changes. What should the admin do?

choices.text: Give Mia the NTFS Full Control permission on `\Projects` so that her file-level rights are higher than the share-level role.
Assign Mia the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role on the file share, keeping her NTFS Modify permission.
Assign Mia the Reader role on the storage account so her share-level and file-level permissions can be merged together.
Assign Mia the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the storage account so that her write requests are authorized.

stem: A storage account uses AD DS authentication for Azure Files. An on-premises service runs as a group Managed Service Account (gMSA) that isn't synced to Microsoft Entra ID, and it must write to a folder on one share. Other users already have role assignments. What should the admin configure at share level?

choices.text: Assign the Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role to the gMSA object directly on the file share.
Assign the Storage File Data SMB Admin role to the gMSA so it can take ownership of the target folder.
Switch the account's identity source to Microsoft Entra Kerberos so that the gMSA gets an Entra identity.
Set a default share-level permission for all authenticated identities, then grant the gMSA NTFS rights.

stem: An administrator created a Standard general-purpose v2 account for a telemetry app. The app now needs consistently low latency for many small block blob writes, so the team asks to switch the account to premium performance. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Open the account's Configuration blade and change Performance from Standard to Premium, then wait for the change to finish
Run `az storage account update --set kind=BlockBlobStorage` to upgrade the existing account in place without copying data
Create a premium block blob account and copy the data with AzCopy, because an account's type can't be changed after creation
Start a redundancy conversion to ZRS, because a conversion moves the account onto the premium solid-state storage tier

stem: An analytics team asks an administrator to enable a hierarchical namespace on an existing general-purpose v2 account that holds production blob data, so Spark jobs can rename directories atomically. Which TWO statements should the administrator include in the change plan? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The upgrade is one-way, so the account can't be turned back to a flat namespace afterward
Existing object replication policies keep replicating blobs after the namespace is enabled
Hadoop jobs that use the WASB driver keep working unchanged and never need the ABFS driver
The upgrade can be undone from the portal within 30 days if an application stops working
Write operations are disabled while the upgrade runs, so a maintenance window is needed

stem: A security baseline turned on Secure transfer required for an account. Since then, a legacy script that uploads nightly reports with a valid SAS to `http://contosorpt.blob.core.windows.net/reports` fails on every request. What should the administrator change to fix it without weakening the baseline?

choices.text: Lower the account's minimum TLS version to TLS 1.0, because the script's older TLS library can't negotiate TLS 1.2
Add the server's public IP to the storage firewall, because secure transfer also blocks traffic from unlisted networks
Change the script's URL to `https://`, because the account now rejects every REST request that arrives over plain HTTP
Allow anonymous blob access on the account, because the SAS is ignored for requests that are sent without encryption

stem: An account was created years ago by a script that never set its minimum TLS version. The administrator must enforce TLS 1.2 but first wants to confirm which TLS version each client application uses, so no client is cut off. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Add a Transactions metric in Metrics Explorer filtered on Authentication equals Anonymous to list the older clients
Connect with Storage Explorer and open the account's properties, which show the TLS versions that clients used
Review the account's activity log, which records the TLS version and caller IP of every read and write request
Send the blob resource logs to a Log Analytics workspace with a diagnostic setting, then query the `TlsVersion` field

stem: A public product catalog loads images over HTTPS from a blob container whose anonymous access level was set to Blob two years ago. This morning every image request without credentials started failing, but no one changed the container. The security team made an account-level change overnight. What explains the failures?

choices.text: The minimum TLS version was raised to 1.2, and anonymous requests can only be negotiated over an older TLS version
Allow Blob anonymous access was disabled on the account, and that account setting overrides the container access level
Secure transfer was enabled, and anonymous requests are always rejected when the account accepts only HTTPS
The Blob access level permits anonymous listing of the container but not reading individual blobs without a SAS

stem: An administrator must move a Standard general-purpose v2 account from LRS to GZRS. Applications must keep reading and writing during the change, and the region supports customer-initiated conversion. Which approach meets the requirement?

choices.text: Change the account to GRS with the portal or `az storage account update --sku`, then start a conversion to GZRS as a separate step
Run one `az storage account update --sku Standard_GZRS` command, which adds zone and geo redundancy together in a single operation
Create a GZRS account, copy all data with AzCopy, then repoint the applications, because LRS accounts can't be converted in place
Initiate a planned failover to the secondary region, which recreates the account as GZRS while the applications keep running

stem: An LRS general-purpose v2 account holds active blobs in the Hot tier plus several thousand older blobs in the Archive tier. The administrator tries to convert it to ZRS and the change can't proceed. What must be done first?

choices.text: Wait 24 hours after the last blob was archived, because conversions are blocked while new Archive tier writes are pending
Enable a hierarchical namespace on the account, because ZRS conversion is supported only for Data Lake Storage accounts
Move the archived blobs to an account whose redundancy supports the Archive tier, then convert the source account to ZRS
Disable blob versioning on the account, because ZRS stores only current versions and can't hold earlier blob versions

stem: A company's GRS general-purpose v2 account serves an order system. Both regions are healthy, and auditors want a disaster recovery drill that makes the secondary region primary without expected data loss and keeps the account geo-redundant afterward. Which failover type fits?

choices.text: Customer-managed planned failover, which swaps the primary and secondary regions and requires both regions to be available
Microsoft-managed failover requested through a support ticket for this one storage account during a planned window
Customer-managed unplanned failover, which promotes the secondary and keeps a geo-redundant copy in the old primary
A redundancy conversion from GRS to RA-GRS, which moves the primary endpoint to the secondary region for testing

stem: A reporting app is configured to read from `contosodata-secondary.blob.core.windows.net` using the account's access key, so reports keep working during a primary outage. Requests to that host fail, while the primary endpoint works. The account's redundancy is GRS. What should the administrator change?

choices.text: Convert the account to GZRS, because the secondary endpoint is available only when the primary region uses zones
Change the account's redundancy to RA-GRS so the secondary endpoint accepts read requests with the existing access keys
Start a customer-managed failover so that the secondary region's endpoint becomes readable for the reporting app
Generate a separate access key for the secondary region, because the secondary endpoint doesn't accept the primary keys

stem: An administrator is setting up object replication of block blobs from a general-purpose v2 account in East US to one in West Europe. Before creating the replication policy, which TWO settings must be enabled? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Container soft delete on both accounts to protect the replicated blobs
A hierarchical namespace on the destination account to hold the replicas
Change feed on the destination account only, so it can request new blobs
Change feed on the source account so changes can be read for replication
Blob versioning on both the source account and the destination account

stem: An administrator created an object replication policy for the container `invoices`. Invoices uploaded after the policy appear in the destination within minutes, but about two million invoices uploaded last year, all in the Hot tier, never show up there. What should the administrator change?

choices.text: Set AllowCrossTenantReplication to true on both accounts, because older blobs are replicated as cross-tenant copies
Set the container pair's copy scope to include existing blobs, because by default a rule copies only new blobs
Enable change feed on the destination account, because older blobs are read from the destination's change feed
Turn on blob versioning on the source account, because existing blobs need a version ID before they can be copied

stem: An administrator is creating a new storage account that must use a customer-managed key in an existing Azure Key Vault that uses the Azure RBAC permission model. Which TWO steps are required? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Generate an elliptic curve (EC) P-256 key in the vault and select it for encryption
Use the new account's system-assigned identity, assigning it Key Vault Administrator first
Give a user-assigned managed identity Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User on the vault
Move the key vault into the same region and subscription as the new storage account
Enable purge protection on the key vault, in addition to soft delete

stem: A software vendor is building one shared storage account that will keep each customer's documents in its own new container. Contracts now require each customer's data to be encrypted with a separate key that can be disabled independently, and uploads must never use another customer's key. What should the administrator configure?

choices.text: Infrastructure encryption on the account, so each container gets its own layer of encryption
Customer-provided keys, with the administrator setting a different key on each container
One customer-managed key for the account, with a new key version for each container
An encryption scope per customer, set as the container's default scope with overrides blocked

stem: A compliance audit requires double encryption at rest for all data in an existing general-purpose v2 account that holds blobs, queues and tables. The account was created without infrastructure encryption. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Create a general-purpose v2 account with infrastructure encryption enabled at creation, then move the data into it
Enable infrastructure encryption on the existing account's Encryption page; data written afterward is double encrypted
Create an encryption scope with infrastructure encryption and make it the default scope for every blob container
Switch the account to a customer-managed key, because combining it with service encryption counts as double encryption

stem: An administrator holds the Owner role on a storage account. She runs `azcopy login`, signs in with her Microsoft Entra account, and runs `azcopy copy` to upload a folder to a container, but the upload fails with an authorization error. What is the most likely fix?

choices.text: Assign her Storage Blob Data Contributor on the account or container and retry after a few minutes
Assign her Storage Account Contributor on the account, which adds the data upload permissions
Add `--recursive=true` to the command, because folder uploads without it are refused as unauthorized
Move the Owner assignment to the subscription scope, because AzCopy checks roles only at that scope

stem: A company runs a Standard tier Azure container registry in West Europe. It is opening a plant in Southeast Asia whose hosts should pull images from a local copy under the same login server, and security wants the registry reachable only through a private endpoint. What should the administrator do?

choices.text: Create a second Standard registry in Southeast Asia, import the images into it, and point a CNAME at the West Europe login server
Change the registry's pricing plan to Premium under Properties, then add a Southeast Asia geo-replication and a private endpoint
Delete the Standard registry and recreate it as Premium with the same name, because a registry's tier is fixed at creation time
Keep the Standard plan, add a Southeast Asia geo-replication, and replace the private endpoint with firewall IP access rules

stem: Policy requires the admin user on a company's Azure container registry to stay disabled. An administrator deploys a Linux container group to Azure Container Instances with a Bicep file that enables its system-assigned managed identity, which has the AcrPull role on the registry. The image pull still fails. What should she do?

choices.text: Wait for the AcrPull role assignment to replicate and redeploy, because system-assigned identity pulls work once the assignment is visible
Give the system-assigned identity the AcrPush role instead, because Container Instances must write cached image layers back to the registry
Give the system-assigned identity a registry control plane role such as Container Registry Contributor, so that it can log in first
Attach a user-assigned managed identity with AcrPull on the registry to the group, and name it in the group's imageRegistryCredentials

stem: A container app on the Consumption plan runs one container with 1.0 vCPU and 2.0Gi of memory. An administrator adds a log-forwarding sidecar container with 0.5 vCPU and 0.5Gi, and the new revision is rejected because of an invalid CPU and memory allocation. Which change fixes the deployment?

choices.text: Size the sidecar at 0.25 vCPU and 0.25Gi so that the app's containers total 1.25 vCPU and 2.25Gi, a smaller pair
Keep both sizes and raise the maximum replica count so that the platform spreads the sidecar's load over more replicas
Size the sidecar at 0.5 vCPU and 1.0Gi so that the app's containers total 1.5 vCPU and 3.0Gi, one of the allowed pairs
Keep both sizes and add a CPU scale rule so that KEDA resizes each replica vertically when the sidecar is under load

stem: An ACR task builds an app image from a Dockerfile whose FROM line is contosoacr.azurecr.io/base/node:20. The task has run successfully many times. The platform team now publishes patched base images as base/node:20.1, base/node:20.2 and so on, and the app image is never rebuilt. What is the cause?

choices.text: Base images in a registry are checked at a random 10-to-60-minute interval, so the rebuild is still waiting in the queue for its next check
Base-image triggers are disabled by default on new tasks, so the administrator must turn on the trigger with the task update command
A base-image trigger fires only when the tag the Dockerfile references is updated, so patches pushed under new version tags never reach the task
ACR tasks track base images only in Docker Hub and Microsoft Container Registry, so a base image in the same registry is never watched

stem: A company upgrades its Azure container registry to Premium and adds geo-replicas in East US and Japan East; the home region is West Europe. Which TWO statements about the geo-replicated registry are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Each replica is a separate registry resource, so role assignments and network rules must be created again in East US and in Japan East
Replication is synchronous, so an image pushed in one region can always be pulled at once from every other replica without retries
Replication is primary-secondary: only West Europe accepts pushes, and the other replicas serve read-only copies of the images
Clients in every region keep using one login server name, and Azure routes each request to a replica with good network performance, usually the closest
If West Europe becomes unavailable, pushes and pulls continue through the other replicas, but registry configuration changes and ACR tasks wait

stem: An administrator runs a nightly report as a container group in Azure Container Instances, created with default settings. The container writes the report and exits with code 0, but it keeps starting again and the group is billed all night. Failed runs must still be retried automatically. What should she do?

choices.text: Delete the container group and create it again with the Never restart policy, which retries failed runs but never restarts finished ones
Delete the container group and create it again with the OnFailure restart policy, because an update can't change the restart policy
Redeploy the group under the same name with the OnFailure restart policy, which updates the policy in place and reuses cached layers
Keep the Always policy and add a liveness probe that fails once the report is written, so that the platform stops the container group

stem: A developer deploys a container group in Azure Container Instances from a YAML file that sets DB_PASSWORD as an environment variable. Anyone with read access sees the password in the portal and in the az container show output. How should the administrator change the deployment?

choices.text: Define DB_PASSWORD with the secureValue property instead of value, so the group's properties show only the variable's name
Set DB_PASSWORD at runtime with az container exec after the group starts, so the deployment file never contains its value
Give readers the Reader role instead of Contributor, because the Reader role shows container properties without their values
Move DB_PASSWORD into an ENV line in the Dockerfile, so the value lives in the image and no longer appears in the group

stem: An administrator wants a container group in Azure Container Instances to keep its output after restarts by mounting an Azure file share at /data. Which TWO statements about this mount are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The share must be an NFS share in a premium storage account, because Azure Container Instances can't mount SMB shares
Files already in the image under /data are merged with the share, so the app sees both sets of files after it starts
The container must run as a non-root user, because the CIFS mount refuses connections from the root account
Only Linux containers can mount an Azure file share, so the image and the group's OS type must be Linux
The mount uses the storage account name, share name and account key, because a managed identity can't mount it

stem: A partner's application calls an API that runs in a container group in Azure Container Instances with a public IP address. The partner hard-coded that IP. After the container group was deleted and recreated, the calls fail. What should the administrator do so this doesn't happen after future redeployments?

choices.text: Always redeploy with az container create under the same group name, which guarantees that the group keeps its IP address
Set a DNS name label on the container group and have the partner use its FQDN, of the form label.region.azurecontainer.io
Change the group's restart policy to Never, because a group that never restarts always keeps the IP address it got
Associate a static Standard public IP address resource directly with the container group's IP address configuration

stem: A container group in Azure Container Instances runs a web container that requests 1 vCPU and a log-shipping container that requests 0.5 vCPU. The web container has short CPU spikes while the log shipper is mostly idle. How is CPU allocated, and what lets the web container use the idle capacity?

choices.text: The group gets 1.5 vCPU, the sum of the requests; add an ACI autoscale rule that adds a web container when CPU passes 80%
The group gets 1.5 vCPU, the sum of the requests; set a resource limit of 3 vCPU on the web container so it can borrow host CPU
The group gets 1.5 vCPU, the sum of the requests; set a resource limit of 1.5 vCPU on the web container so it can use idle CPU
The group gets 1 vCPU, the largest request, shared by both; raise the web container's request to 2 vCPU with an in-place update

stem: A team runs a container app with external ingress in the default revision mode. It wants to send 10% of user traffic to a new image version for a day, keep 90% on the current revision, and roll back quickly if errors rise. What should the administrator configure?

choices.text: Switch the app to multiple revision mode, deploy the new image as a new revision, and set the traffic weights to 90 and 10
Create a staging deployment slot on the container app and set its traffic percentage to 10 in the deployment slot settings
Keep single revision mode and give the new revision a 10% weight, because single mode keeps the old revision until traffic moves
Deploy the new image as a second container app with internal ingress, and set the environment to split traffic 90 to 10

stem: An administrator deploys a container app that processes messages from an Azure Service Bus queue. Ingress is disabled, minimum replicas is 0, and no scale rule was added. Messages pile up in the queue and the app shows zero running replicas. What should the administrator do to fix this while still allowing scale to zero?

choices.text: Raise the maximum number of replicas from 10 to 30, so that the platform has enough room to start replicas when messages arrive
Add an HTTP scale rule with concurrentRequests set to 1, so that the first message that arrives in the queue starts a new replica
Add a custom scale rule of type azure-servicebus with the queue name and a message count, authenticated with a secret or managed identity
Lower the KEDA polling interval to 5 seconds, so that the platform checks the queue more often and starts a replica sooner

stem: A company is creating a new Azure Container Apps environment for an internal HR app. The app must be reachable from virtual machines in a virtual network and from on-premises users over a site-to-site VPN, but never from the internet. How should the administrator configure it?

choices.text: Create the environment as internal in a subnet of the virtual network, and set the app's ingress to internal, limited to the environment
Create the environment as internal in a subnet of the virtual network, and set the app's ingress to external, accepting traffic from anywhere
Create the environment with a public inbound IP for testing, and change its accessibility level to internal before the app goes live
Create the environment with a public inbound IP, and set the app's ingress to internal, limited to the Container Apps environment
